_note: Quiz and true-or-false items written but not yet blind-checked; apply_check.py moves checked items onto the site.

item.statement: Beliefs can shift after a psychedelic retreat and still be shifted 6 months on.
item.why: In one study, belief in things like other worlds rose a little and was still up 6 months on. But only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey, and most already leaned that way.

item.statement: It's been shown that psilocybin can change your personality.
item.why: Not proven. People rated themselves a little more open after, but the one test against another drug found no difference.

item.statement: People whose beliefs change after a trip start to believe in bad luck too.
item.why: In a survey of 1,606 such people, belief in bad luck from black cats didn't rise. Belief that plants can be conscious did, as they recalled it years later.

item.statement: The simple shapes people see on LSD have been sorted into just four types.
item.why: Lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals. Similar visions also come with flickering light or when falling asleep.

item.statement: In a lab study, all who took psilocybin came out more 'open'.
item.why: About a third of the volunteers scored lower afterwards. On average, scores rose by under 3 points.

item.statement: It's proven that trip tunnels and spirals come from the brain's wiring.
item.why: A maths model suggests it, but it wasn't tested in people on a drug.

item.statement: Most men get harder erections on MDMA.
item.why: In one survey of 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker on MDMA and 8 said stronger. They were remembering past experiences, and nobody tested their pills.

item.statement: In one survey, most men who had used MDMA before sex said orgasm took longer.
item.why: 16 of 20 men said so, and 6 of 15 women, yet 32 of 35 people said they were more satisfied. It's one small survey of people remembering the past.

item.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
item.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

item.statement: In a lab study, MDA brought more visions than MDMA, but less anxiety.
item.why: That's what 12 people on MDA reported, set against MDMA results from other people in earlier studies, so it's a weak comparison.

item.statement: In a lab study, MDA's effects lasted longer than MDMA's.
item.why: Still felt at 8 hours, while MDMA had faded by 6. But MDMA was only watched for 6 hours, in other people.

item.statement: In a lab test, LSD and psilocybin trips felt much alike. The big difference was how long they lasted.
item.why: In 28 people, LSD lasted about 9 to 11 hours and psilocybin 6 to 7. Ratings barely differed, but that's no proof they're the same.

item.statement: Adding MDMA to LSD has been shown to make a bad trip less likely.
item.why: In 24 people, bad-feeling and fear scores weren't clearly lower than on LSD alone, and nobody tested it at a party.

item.statement: Most people can't tell LSD from psilocybin if not told which they got.
item.why: By the 28-person study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, though the trips were rated alike.

item.statement: Taking MDMA with alcohol makes you feel less drunk.
item.why: In a lab study of 9 men, MDMA took away alcohol's sleepiness, not the drunk feeling, and test scores still dropped.

item.statement: Taking MDMA with LSD pushes heart rate and blood pressure higher than LSD alone.
item.why: In a lab study of 24 people, they rose about as high as on MDMA alone. Body temperature wasn't clearly higher.

item.statement: With MDMA, blood alcohol was a bit lower, yet people felt just as drunk.
item.why: 15% lower at its peak, in 9 men, but drunk ratings didn't fall, and test scores at their worst dropped about as much.

item.statement: By late 2021, about 15 in 100 overdose deaths in the western US showed signs of fake pills.
item.why: That was up from about 5 in 100 in mid-2019. Death records likely miss many fake pills, so the true share may be higher.

item.statement: In US overdose deaths with signs of fake pills, most fakes copied oxycodone.
item.why: In 2021 records, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30'. Death records likely miss many fake pills.

item.statement: Even experts often said a short overdose story did not tell them enough.
item.why: They said so in about a quarter of their answers. It was one small US study, using written stories, not real overdoses.

item.statement: Trained people spotted every opioid overdose on a paper test.
item.why: They spotted about 7 of 9, against about 5 of 9 for people without training. It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked.

item.statement: Pills sold as ecstasy have nearly always held MDMA.
item.why: In European tests in 2009, as few as 19 in 100 pills held MDMA in one country. These were pills people chose to bring in.

item.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
item.why: One review describes two studies of people on methadone: their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

item.statement: In one study, people who stayed to the end of a detox programme had fewer overdose deaths later.
item.why: The opposite: all 3 overdose deaths came among the 37 who finished it, and none among the 100 who left earlier. The researchers suspect lost tolerance, but nobody measured it.

item.statement: In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place than in the usual one.
item.why: In one researcher's rat studies, yes. In people, it has only been looked at in 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with.

item.statement: Death rates were about the same in and out of methadone treatment.
item.why: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. People who leave differ in other ways, so this can't show cause.

item.statement: You can't die from opioid withdrawal.
item.why: Deaths have been reported, all in jail, linked to vomiting and diarrhoea that dried people out and went untreated. How often it happens is unknown: the list comes from one editorial.

item.statement: Big studies of people show a new place makes an overdose more likely.
item.why: In people, there's one study: 10 overdose survivors recalling the day about 5 years later. Only 3 recalled a new place or crowd.

item.statement: The first weeks off methadone were the riskiest time in studies.
item.why: In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against 6 in steady treatment. People who leave may differ in other ways.
